Mitochondrial Disorders
Etiology and Clinical Manifestations
Mitochondria are essential for the production of energy in all 
types of tissues. Th ey are found in all cells in the body (except
mature red blood cells) and are considered the “power houses”
or energy producers of the cell. Mitochondrial disorders result 
either from defects of the respiratory chain that produces energy 
or from defects aﬀ ecting the overall number and function of the 
mitochondria. A defect in function of the mitochondrial system 
results in diseases aﬀ ecting multiple organs with a wide range
of symptoms, including cardiomyopathy, blindness, deafness, 
endocrine problems, and muscle disorders. Individuals present-
ing with a mitochondrial disorder can range from infants, as in
the case of Leigh’s disease, to adults with progressive neurologic
or muscle disorders. Table 26.13 lists the spectrum of conditions
associated with mitochondrial mutations leading to disruption
in function. Mitochondrial disorders are renowned for their
variability in clinical features and genetic causes, making it dif-
ﬁ cult to determine their true prevalence.65, 66
